prompt: In the triangle construction from 3-SAT to Independent Set, why is the target the number of clauses rather than the number of distinct variables?

options.text: Each variable can be selected only once
options.explanation: Vertices represent occurrences; compatible occurrences of the same literal can be selected in different clauses.

options.text: At most one pick per triangle plus that target forces every clause to contribute
options.explanation: This gives a chosen literal in each clause, which is essential to reconstructing a satisfying assignment.

options.text: The graph contains one vertex per variable
options.explanation: It contains one vertex per literal occurrence.

options.text: A smaller target always proves unsatisfiability
options.explanation: A smaller target can ignore clauses, so its success need not imply satisfiability.

workedExample: A triangle permits at most one selected occurrence from its clause. Asking for as many selected vertices as clauses therefore forces a pick from every triangle. Counting distinct variables instead could allow the algorithm to skip clauses, breaking the inference from an independent set to a satisfying assignment.

prompt: A SAT-to-Independent-Set implementation builds all clause triangles but forgets an edge between opposite occurrences of the same variable. Which guarantee is threatened?

options.text: A satisfying assignment must now create an edge between its true picks
options.explanation: Removing an edge cannot invalidate an independent set that previously worked.

options.text: Selected literals may no longer extend to a consistent truth assignment
options.explanation: Opposite occurrences can now both be selected, so graph choices need not describe one assignment.

options.text: Two vertices from the same triangle can be picked
options.explanation: Triangle edges are still present and forbid that.

options.text: The graph is too large to construct in polynomial time
options.explanation: Omitting an edge changes correctness, not the polynomial size bound.

workedExample: An independent set must correspond to compatible truth choices. Without the edge between a positive occurrence and a negative occurrence of the same variable, both could be selected. Each clause triangle still limits local picks, but the selections may not extend to one global assignment.
